strengths: Clear, well-motivated question (when does behavioral diversity beat homogeneous teams in cooperative MARL?) that has received mostly empirical treatment in prior work; the paper supplies a principled, reward-design perspective that is genuinely missing from the literature.

Elegant theoretical contribution: the characterization of the heterogeneity gain ΔR via Schur-convexity/concavity of the inner and outer aggregation operators is clean, and the theorems (3.1–3.3) come with correct, complete proofs in the appendix. The reduction to a simple convexity test for sum-form aggregators (App. E) makes the theory practically usable, and the {min, mean, max} table (Fig. 2) gives crisp, verifiable predictions.

The experiments are carefully designed to test the theory: the matrix games exactly recover the theoretically derived gains for all nine aggregator combinations (Tabs. 5–8), and the embodied Multi-Goal-Capture experiments show the curvature predictions transfer to long-horizon MARL. Multiple seeds (9–13) and deviation reporting are provided.

HED is a reasonable algorithmic contribution (gradient-based environment design maximizing empirical heterogeneity gain), and its ability to rediscover the theoretically optimal softmax/power-sum parameterizations (Fig. 5) provides mutual validation of both theory and algorithm. The observability–heterogeneity trade-off analysis (Fig. 4b) is a nice additional insight connecting neural vs. behavioral heterogeneity.

Good positioning relative to related work (behavioral diversity, task allocation, environment co-design), and honest treatment of limitations (App. L), including the separability assumption, differentiability requirement of HED, and the reward-centric nature of the analysis.
Strong reproducibility: code with Hydra configs attached, compute resources documented, hyperparameters specified.
weaknesses: The core theory, while elegant, applies relatively standard majorization/Schur-convexity machinery to a fairly restricted model: instantaneous, separable, non-spatial task allocation with symmetric aggregators and fixed effort budgets. Several results (e.g., Thm. 3.2, 3.3) are near-direct consequences of well-known Schur properties, and the scope of settings where the theory is formally applicable is narrow relative to the motivating vision (acknowledged in App. L).
Theorem 3.4 provides only lower bounds on the softmax heterogeneity gain; the conjecture that the bound is exact is unproven, which slightly weakens the 'exact characterizations' narrative.

There is an important gap between the theory (optimal allocations exist and ΔR > 0) and the empirical claims: in Multi-Goal-Capture, the reported gains depend on learning dynamics and asymmetric learnability (e.g., unique vs. continuum of good homogeneous policies), and negative empirical gains appear for theoretically ∆R = 0 cases. The paper acknowledges this, but it means the experiments partly measure learning-facility rather than the structural heterogeneity advantage the theory characterizes, muddying the validation story.

HED's novelty is moderate: it is essentially gradient ascent on environment parameters through a differentiable simulator, closely related to differentiable-simulation policy training and to PAIRED-style environment design; the main novel element is the heterogeneity-gain objective rather than the algorithmic machinery. Moreover, HED's validation is largely 'rediscovers what the theory already predicts' in the same small environments, rather than demonstrating discovery of genuinely new tasks where heterogeneity matters.

Experimental scale is limited: matrix games with N=M ∈ {2,4}, a simple 2-goal navigation environment, and small N, M for HED. No comparison against alternative diversity-promoting methods (e.g., ID-injection, hypernetworks, diversity intrinsic rewards) that the paper surveys, so the practical usefulness of designing rewards via curvature/HED relative to existing techniques remains untested.

The practical significance of 'maximizing heterogeneity gain' as a design goal is somewhat under-argued: it is not clear when a practitioner would want to search for the reward structure that most benefits heterogeneous teams versus simply choosing a known appropriate reward (e.g., U=min, T=max for coverage), and the discussion of this point is brief.

strengths: The central question—when does behavioral heterogeneity provably help in cooperative multi-agent task allocation—is well-motivated and clearly framed from a reward-design perspective, filling a genuine gap since prior MARL diversity methods presume heterogeneity is advantageous without characterizing when it is.

The theoretical treatment is clean: the Schur-convexity/Schur-concavity criteria for the inner and outer aggregators (Thms. 3.1–3.3) are correct (proofs in App. F appear sound), and the sum-form reduction (Lemma E.1, Cor. E.1) makes the curvature test practical.

The matrix-game experiments exhaustively cover all nine {min, mean, max} aggregator combinations and match the theoretical predictions essentially exactly, in both continuous and discrete allocation regimes, over multiple seeds.
The observability–heterogeneity trade-off experiment (Fig. 4b) is a nice empirical touch that connects the reward-curvature theory to the known neural vs. behavioral heterogeneity distinction.

Reproducibility is above average: code, YAML configs, plot scripts, and compute estimates are provided, and the limitations section (App. L) is candid about theoretical scope (separable tasks, reward-centric analysis) and the differentiability requirement of HED.
weaknesses: Limited theoretical depth: Theorems 3.1–3.3 are fairly direct applications of classical majorization/Schur-convexity results (the paper itself cites [39, 40]), and the analysis is confined to a static, separable, non-spatial allocation model; the interesting embodied, time-extended case is handled only empirically, not theoretically.
Theorem 3.4 provides only lower bounds, and the authors concede the conjectured exact value is unproven—so the flagship parameterized-family result is incomplete.

The HED algorithm is a rather straightforward combination of differentiable-simulation backpropagation (e.g., [42, 43]) with standard MARL training (MAPPO), closely paralleling PAIRED-style co-design [36]; the claimed novelty over [35, 36] is modest, and the claimed ability to 'discover previously unknown types of tasks' is not demonstrated—HED is only validated by rediscovering reward regimes already predicted by the theory.

Experimental scale and breadth are limited: matrix games with N = M = 2 and 4, and one bespoke embodied environment (Multi-Goal-Capture); no comparison against existing heterogeneous-MARL or environment-design baselines, and no demonstration on standard benchmarks (e.g., LBF is only analyzed in the appendix, not run).

Empirical heterogeneity gains conflate reward-structure effects with optimization/learning-dynamics effects (e.g., the negative gains for U = max, T = min are attributed to homogeneous teams learning faster), which weakens the claim that the observed gains validate the theory rather than the training budget; the authors acknowledge this but do not resolve it.

The practical payoff is unclear: knowing the sign of ΔR requires already knowing the reward structure, so the decision-relevant use case (choosing parameter sharing vs. heterogeneous policies for a given task) is only indirectly addressed.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored and well-motivated question in MARL: when do reward structures make behavioral heterogeneity advantageous? Prior diversity methods presume heterogeneity helps; this work supplies a principled characterization, which is a real conceptual gap filled.

The core theoretical insight is elegant and actionable: the heterogeneity gain is governed by the Schur-convexity/concavity of nested (inner/outer) aggregation operators, and for sum-form aggregators this reduces to a simple convexity test. This gives practitioners a computable diagnostic (Thms. 3.1–3.3, Corollary E.1, the {min, mean, max} table).

The experiments are well designed to test the theory: the nine {min, mean, max} combinations in both discrete and continuous matrix games recover the theoretically predicted gains (Tables 5–8), and the theory transfers to a long-horizon embodied environment (Multi-Goal-Capture). The observability-heterogeneity trade-off experiment (Fig. 4b) is a nice addition connecting reward curvature to the known neural-vs-behavioral heterogeneity distinction.

HED is a reasonable and useful algorithmic contribution: gradient-based co-design of environment parameters to maximize/minimize the empirical heterogeneity gain, and it rediscovers the theoretically optimal aggregator parameterizations in both Softmax and Power-Sum families (Fig. 5), providing mutual validation of theory and algorithm.

Reproducibility is strong: code with Hydra configs and plotting scripts is attached, compute usage is reported, multiple seeds (9–13) with mean/std are reported, and the limitations/open-questions appendix (App. L) is honest and substantive.
Connections to known environments (Colonel Blotto, level-based foraging) in App. D demonstrate the framework's applicability beyond the custom testbeds.
weaknesses: The theoretical scope is fairly narrow. Results apply to separable tasks with a double-aggregation (inner/outer) reward structure in a non-spatial, instantaneous allocation model; the analysis of the outer aggregator requires a constant-sum normalization assumption (Thm. 3.3). The MARL connection is informal — a positive ΔR is only 'evidence' of an advantage for embodied learners, not a guarantee, so the headline claim connecting curvature to MARL is weaker than it first appears.

The core mathematical insight, while clean, is arguably unsurprising: Schur-convexity/concavity and majorization are standard tools, and the conclusion that inequality-amplifying inner aggregators plus uniformity-amplifying outer aggregators favor specialization is fairly intuitive. Proofs (App. F) are straightforward applications of majorization.
Theorem 3.4 provides only lower bounds, with the exact value left as an unproven conjecture; this limits the precision of the parameterized-family analysis.

Experiments are small-scale: N = M ∈ {2, 4} in matrix games and N = M = 2-ish in Multi-Goal-Capture; no scaling study of how the gain behaves for larger teams/tasks, and only MAPPO is used. The empirical gains in the embodied setting deviate from theory and are partly attributed to learning dynamics (e.g., unique vs. continuum of homogeneous optima), which is interesting but means the validation is qualitative in that regime.

HED's novelty relative to prior environment/co-design work (PAIRED, differentiable-simulation approaches) is incremental: it is essentially regret-gradient environment design with a heterogeneous-vs-homogeneous team objective. It is also validated only on reward-parameter search in one environment family; the claimed generality (e.g., optimizing obstacle placements) is not demonstrated.

Some results reported as confirmations are near-tautological for the discrete case (e.g., Table 8 gains match theory exactly with zero variance), and the practical significance of 'aggregators that maximize heterogeneity' beyond the tested navigation scenario is not established.

strengths: The paper addresses an interesting and well-motivated question — when behavioral heterogeneity is advantageous in cooperative MARL — that is orthogonal to most prior work on how to induce diversity, and gives a principled answer via reward design.

The theoretical framework is clean and elegant: modeling team rewards as a double aggregation R(A) = U(T_1(a_1),...,T_M(a_M)) and characterizing the heterogeneity gain ΔR via Schur-convexity/Schur-concavity of the aggregators yields simple, checkable criteria (and collapses to a convexity test for sum-form aggregators). Theorems 3.1–3.3 plus the min/mean/max table and softmax bounds (Thm 3.4) are coherent, and the proofs in App. G appear correct and complete.

Strong empirical validation strategy: results in a controlled matrix game match theoretical predictions exactly (for multiple N=M values and both discrete/continuous allocations), and the theory transfers qualitatively to embodied, long-horizon settings (Multi-goal-capture, 2v2 tag, VMAS football), including a sparse-reward case and a case where the aggregator structure is only part of the reward.

HetGPS is a well-motivated complement to the theory: a differentiable-simulation bilevel method that rediscovers the theoretically optimal aggregator parameterizations (Softmax and Power-Sum), is robust to adversarial initialization (App. Q), and has modest overhead (~25%). This closes the loop between theory and learned reward design.

Good reproducibility practices: code and YAML configs attached, seeds and variance reported (8–13 seeds in most experiments), compute estimates provided, honest limitations section (App. R), and analysis of neural vs. behavioral heterogeneity and the observability trade-off (App. N) that anticipates likely reviewer concerns.

The paper is generally well-written, with informative figures (e.g., Fig. 7 rollouts, Fig. 5 HetGPS parameter evolution) and interpretable aggregator semantics (e.g., U=min, T=max = 'cover all goals with different agents').
weaknesses: The core theoretical results are technically modest. Schur-convexity via majorization is classical, and Theorems 3.1–3.3 follow from fairly direct applications of the majorization order plus monotonicity; the 'curvature determines heterogeneity gain' conclusion is arguably intuitive. The contribution is more a useful reframing than deep mathematics, which may limit impact for a theory-focused audience.

The theory is restricted to instantaneous, reward-centric task allocation with symmetric, monotone aggregators and effort-summing constraints. The empirical embodied settings only satisfy the framework's assumptions approximately (proximity-based efforts, time-extended dynamics, reward shaping), so the MARL 'validation' is qualitative ('theory reliably predicts when there is a gain') rather than exact — the numeric gains deviate and can even be negative due to learning dynamics (e.g., Table 9, Fig. 4a), which somewhat dilutes the strength of the theory-to-practice claim.

The theoretical analysis cannot explain transition-dynamics-driven heterogeneity, which the authors themselves flag as an open question; the framework may not cover important domains (multi-robot manipulation, etc.).

HetGPS is evaluated only on one environment family (Multi-goal-capture) with two aggregator families, and only against the paper's own theory — there are no comparisons to alternative environment-design baselines (e.g., PAIRED-style or Designer-RL variants adapted to this objective), so its empirical superiority is asserted rather than demonstrated. The non-differentiable variant is discussed but never tested.

Some experimental concerns: only 4 seeds for the observability experiment (Fig. 11), a small number for the adversarial initialization study (3 seeds), and the N=M=8 negative gains for predicted-zero structures are explained post hoc by training budget rather than analyzed more rigorously.

Practical significance is somewhat limited so far: the main actionable takeaway (use concave outer / convex inner aggregators, e.g., min/max, to encourage specialization) is a fairly narrow slice of reward design, and the paper does not demonstrate the theory improving performance on a benchmark task relative to standard reward choices beyond the studied aggregator grid.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and clearly articulated question: characterizing which reward structures create an incentive for behavioral heterogeneity, which is orthogonal to the large literature on how to induce diversity in MARL.

The theoretical framework is clean and elegant: the double-aggregation abstraction R(A) = U(T_1(a_1),...,T_M(a_M)) is general, and the connection between Schur-convexity/concavity of the aggregators and the sign of the heterogeneity gain is a tidy, interpretable criterion (Thms. 3.1-3.3), with useful special cases (min/mean/max table, softmax bounds in Thm. 3.4, sum-form corollary).

Experiments are reasonably thorough: matrix games with all nine aggregator pairs exactly recover the theoretical gains, results are replicated across N = M = 2, 4, 8, and the curvature test is probed in embodied settings (multi-goal-capture, tag, football), including the case where the aggregator structure is only a component of the total reward.

The observation-heterogeneity trade-off experiment (App. N) nicely distinguishes neural from behavioral heterogeneity and connects to prior findings, and the paper includes code, configuration files, compute details, and a candid limitations appendix.
weaknesses: Limited theoretical depth/novelty: the core results are direct applications of classical majorization and Schur-convexity (Roberts & Varberg; Peajcariaac & Tong) to a two-level aggregation of a product of simplices. The theorems are short and the proofs straightforward; the interesting regime (time-extended, embodied, non-spatially trivial allocations) is precisely where the formal analysis does not apply, so the 'main insight' covers only the simplest instantiation of the problem.

The theoretical-to-practical bridge is weaker than claimed. In Multi-goal-capture, theory is said to 'reliably predict' gains, yet empirically observed gains differ numerically and even in sign from theory (negative gains for (max,min) and (max,mean) attributed to learning-dynamics artifacts). The football experiment only satisfies the double-aggregation structure partially and adds reward shaping, so it is a qualitative sanity check rather than a validation. The repeated reliance on 'learning dynamics' explanations suggests the theory predicts only a coarse sign pattern.

The algorithmic contribution (HetGPS) is modest: it is a fairly standard bilevel loop combining MAPPO with gradient-based environment parameter search via a differentiable simulator, closely following PAIRED and Gao et al. (2024) with the protagonist/antagonist replaced by het/hom teams. It is only ever validated by confirming that it rediscovers the aggregator parameterizations already predicted by the theory; no comparison against alternative environment-design baselines (e.g., PAIRED-style RL designers, evolutionary search) is provided.

Empirical evaluation has gaps: the HetGPS experiments involve only two parameterized aggregator families in a single environment, with largely unconstrained softmax parameters whose saturation is acknowledged; the tag environment uses heuristic (non-learning) escapees; several claims in the main text end mid-sentence ('visuals available', 'find more visualizations on'), indicating incomplete writing.

Significance is bounded by scope: the framework requires that agent contributions be expressible as scalar efforts per task, which excludes many multi-agent domains (manipulation, communication-rich settings), and the practical payoff — knowing whether to use parameter sharing vs. independent networks given a reward structure — is not directly demonstrated on any standard benchmark or against existing diversity-inducing methods.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and previously under-theorized question: which reward structures create incentives for behavioral (rather than neural) heterogeneity in cooperative MARL. This 'when' question is a genuine complement to the large 'how' literature on promoting diversity, and the positioning in Sec. 1.1 is clear and honest about this framing.

The core theoretical result — that the heterogeneity gain ΔR is governed by Schur-convexity/Schur-concavity of the inner and outer aggregation operators — is clean, interpretable, and practically actionable. The reduction to a simple convexity test for sum-form aggregators (App. F, Corollary F.1) and the exact min/mean/max gain table (Fig. 2) make the theory directly usable for reward design.

The experiments are unusually thorough for this kind of theory paper: the theory is validated in one-shot matrix games (N=M=2,4,8, discrete and continuous), then transferred to embodied, long-horizon environments (Multi-goal-capture, 2v2 tag, VMAS football), including a control experiment showing the curvature test remains predictive when R(A) is only a component of a larger shaped reward (Tab. 10). The exact match between predicted and learned gains is convincing evidence.

HetGPS is a sensible and well-executed algorithmic contribution: gradient-based bilevel optimization of underspecified environment parameters, validated both by rediscovering theoretically optimal aggregator parameterizations (Fig. 5) and by robustness to adversarial initialization (App. Q). The discussion of Stackelberg structure and differentiable-simulation advantages (App. P) is appropriate.

Good attention to the neural vs. behavioral heterogeneity distinction, including the observability-heterogeneity trade-off experiment (App. N), which honestly delimits the scope of the theory (it concerns what is achievable, not what learning dynamics will converge to).
Reproducibility is strong: code with per-experiment YAML configs, plotting scripts, compute estimates, and honest disclosure of LLM usage and limitations (App. R).
weaknesses: The mathematical depth of the theory is moderate. The main theorems follow fairly directly from classical majorization/Schur-convexity arguments (Roberts & Varberg; Peajcariaac & Tong), and Theorem 3.3 requires the restrictive constant-sum task-scores assumption. The contribution is a well-executed application of known tools rather than new mathematical machinery, which limits the paper's theoretical impact.

The framework is reward-centric and restricted to effort-allocation-structured rewards. The authors acknowledge (App. R) that settings where heterogeneity helps due to transition dynamics (e.g., multi-robot manipulation) are not covered, which bounds the scope of the central claim 'when is diversity rewarded'.

Theory–practice gaps are acknowledged but notable: in N=M=8 and some embodied settings, empirically heterogeneous teams show negative gains under fixed training budgets, so the exact-match claims hold mainly in regimes where learning has converged. The claim that learned policies 'recover the exact gains' should be qualified more prominently in the main text.

HetGPS is validated only on a single environment family (Multi-goal-capture) with two parametrized aggregator families where the theoretical optimum is already known. The most interesting use case — discovering heterogeneity-favorable configurations in settings where theory does not apply — is not demonstrated; the non-differentiable-environment variant is discussed but untested.

Practical significance for reward design is asserted more than demonstrated: the paper does not include a case study showing that a real MARL practitioner, using the curvature test, designs a better-performing system (e.g., improved sample efficiency or final return under a resource constraint) compared to existing heterogeneity/parameter-sharing methods.

Some empirical variance is high (e.g., Tab. 10 football gains of 1.76 ± 0.72; Tab. 9 entry −0.75 ± 0.5), and seed counts in some appendix experiments (3–4 seeds) are thin for the strength of the conclusions drawn.
